groundTruthNarrative: On the morning of 9 Sept, Brannock Civils isolated Millbrook Low's Station Road main for renewal. To hold pressure in east Millbrook, they charged a temporary 80 mm overland hose from hydrant AG-417 on Kestrel Road, on the Ashgrove side, to hydrant ML-112 in Millbrook. Ashgrove runs at a higher pressure (PRV 4.0 bar) than Millbrook (3.0 bar), so about 8.5 L/s of Ashgrove water has flowed through the hose into Millbrook ever since. Millbrook's own inlet flow fell by the same amount in the same minutes, and the two districts' combined inflow did not change. The extra flow through Ashgrove's inlet main and network increased headloss, so Beacon Hill pressures fell below the service level. The PRV held its setpoint throughout; it simply opened further. The boundary-valve check was correct but incomplete: it covered pipe connections and control's records, and the hose was in neither. The Station Road main was recommissioned on 27 Sept, but the hose was left connected, so the transfer continues. There is no burst under the rail cutting. The consultant's model fitted an outflow near that section only because no other outflow locations were tested, and Kestrel Road lies at the same end of the network. Whether the contractor told network control on 9 Sept cannot be settled: the diary claim was written up later, the permit field is completed only at close-out, the control-room log was taken up by the Northfield burst, and calls were not being recorded.

answers.rationale: C4 shows Millbrook's inflow fell by 8.4 L/s in the same minutes that Ashgrove's rose by 8.6 L/s, and the two districts' combined inflow is unchanged within meter uncertainty. The extra Ashgrove inflow is therefore being delivered into Millbrook, not lost, which leaves no room for a burst of meaningful size. E6's survey also found only 0.4 L/s of leakage. C13's model fit does not tell a burst apart from any other outflow at that end of the network.

Using S1 evidence only: E2 shows a sudden, lasting 8.6 L/s rise in night flow, the classic burst pattern. E4 and C1 rule out a PRV fault. E5 and C6 report the only mapped boundary connections checked and sealing. E5 also records that network control had no temporary cross-boundary links (including hose or hydrant links) or works cross-feeds on record, so the same-day Station Road start (E3) has no known path into Millbrook. E3, C3, C7 and C12 rule out a demand increase, and C10 records an old, failure-prone trunk main. Once the PRV, demand and transfer rivals are each checked and excluded at S1, a leak fits better than any rival.

E4 shows the PRV outlet at 3.97–4.03 bar throughout, including after the service and after 9 Sept. The valve opened further, as it should when more flow passes through. The pressure loss happens downstream of a PRV that is holding its setpoint.

C4 shows Ashgrove's rise mirrored minute-for-minute by Millbrook's fall, with combined inflow flat. C5 identifies the path: a hose from an Ashgrove hydrant into a Millbrook hydrant, charged on 9 Sept and still connected after 27 Sept. E5's check is not wrong, but it covered mapped pipe connections and control's records only. A hydrant-to-hydrant hose that was not on control's records falls outside both.

Using S1 evidence only: E5 and C6 record that GIS lists four pipe connections as the only links between the districts, and all four were physically confirmed shut with pressure differences holding across them. E5 also records that network control checked and had no temporary cross-boundary links, explicitly including hose or hydrant links, or works cross-feeds on record for Ashgrove or its neighbours. The Station Road works in E3 started the same day, but the record of agreed continuity arrangements (the channel E3's permit condition requires) shows no cross-feed, so at S1 there is no evidenced path. Both mapped and temporary links were checked, so the S1 evidence counts against a cross-district transfer.

The rise happened within four minutes at 06:40 on a single day and appears in night flow. It continued after the heatwave ended on 13 Sept, and no other DMA shows it (E2). Fenwick Fields was fully connected by 29 Aug, before the 1–8 Sept baseline (E3). Demand growth does not produce a lasting step like this.

The contractor's diary says they called control and got approval, but that entry was written up on 4 Oct, after the investigation contacted them. The blank permit §7 is explained by the permit still being open. Control having nothing on record (E5) does not show that no call was made: C8 shows the log covered only the Northfield burst during that window, calls were not recorded, and the duty controller has not been interviewed. The evidence does not point either way.

Temporal order: the hose was charged early on 9 Sept (C5), and the steps followed at 06:38–06:44 (C4, E2). Mechanism: a hose from higher-pressure Ashgrove into lower-pressure Millbrook (C5), with extra flow raising headloss in Ashgrove. Covariation: Millbrook's fall matches Ashgrove's rise. Main rival excluded: combined inflow is flat, so there is no burst (C4). Without C5 the link would be association-only.

The PRV outlet held 4.0 bar from the 5 Sept service until 9 Sept and afterwards (E4, C1). Pressure and flow changed four days after the service, at 06:40 on 9 Sept, with no setpoint change or override. This counts against the link itself.

All Fenwick Fields homes were connected by 29 Aug, before the 1–8 Sept baseline of 6.2–6.4 L/s (E3, E2). The step happened in four minutes on 9 Sept, with no connection event then. C3 gives a design night demand of 0.05 L/s for the whole development.

C5 identifies the connection and records that Millbrook went back on its own feed on 27 Sept, so the stated condition is met and Millbrook will not lose supply. C4 confirms this connection accounts for the extra flow. Removing the hose is cheap, reversible and directly testable on both meters and the logger. It is the best next step.

Going to 4.8 bar overrides the PM-7 cap of 4.2 bar. The cap exists because the last rise to 4.6 bar produced 14 bursts in six weeks on Ashgrove's cast-iron mains (E4). Under the supported explanation it also pushes more Ashgrove water through the hose into Millbrook and leaves the cause in place. No live rival explanation makes it safe.

The notice would be justified if H5 were confirmed, since the permit condition requires agreement with network control (E3). But whether the contractor called is unresolved (C5, C8). A notice can be withdrawn if the controller later confirms the call, so acting now is premature rather than harmful.

Customers have been below the service reference level for weeks (E1), so communicating with them is reasonable and harmless. But E6 records that customer services already texted every Beacon Hill and Ridgeway customer on 16 and 29 Sept and keep a web notice updated, so a further letter adds little and does nothing to restore pressure. It is reasonable but not among the best next actions.

With C5 the transfer path is located and Millbrook is known not to need it. With C4 the transfer is shown to account for the whole flow rise. Together they justify committing to A1 now. From the initial file alone, a transfer looks ruled out and no path is known.

authoringNotes: Revision 2 (post-review): (1) S14 was ruled ambiguous because writing to customers could be called 'preferred' as a cheap parallel step. E6 now records that customer services already texted every Beacon Hill and Ridgeway customer on 16 and 29 Sept and keep a web notice updated, and A4 now reads 'Send a further letter', so it is reasonable but adds little and only 'acceptable' fits. (2) The presenting request is moved from 1 Oct to 6 Oct, and stage S2 is defined as 16 Sept to 5 Oct, so the 3 Oct and 4 Oct entries in C5 fall before the decision point. (3) As the adjudicator suggested, E5's control query now explicitly covers 'hose or hydrant links', which removes the misreading behind the blind 'unknown' answers on S02 and S05. Earlier revision: E5 records that network control had no temporary cross-boundary links or works cross-feeds on record, so at S1 the transfer rival was checked through both channels (mapped pipe connections and the continuity-arrangement record the permit condition requires). That makes H3 contradicted and H1 supported at S1. This fits C8 (no Station Road entry; calls unrecorded) and leaves H5 unknown, because 'not on record' does not mean 'not informed' when the log was taken up with the Northfield burst. Stage change: at S1, a leak is the best-supported explanation and a cross-district transfer is counted against. The S2 reads C4 and C5 reverse both. E6 (S2, in the initial file) restates the leak case through a confident manager narrative. Non-redundancy: C4 alone settles H1 as contradicted, through the matched volumes and flat combined inflow. C5 does not quantify the hose flow and gives date-level timing only, so with C5 alone a leak in the unsurveyed section is still possible. C5 alone settles R1 as causal (mechanism) and SUFF/A1 (path located; Millbrook's main back in service). C4 alone leaves R1 association-only and the path unknown. No other item reveals the hose or Millbrook's flow: C11 hints at an interruption and restoration but gives no path or volume, and C13 is a trap (a fit limited to the brief). H5 stays unknown on every read path. A2 is harmful under the only live causal explanation because it overrides a documented burst-protection cap. A3 is reversible, so it is keyed premature, not harmful. R2 and R3 are contradicted on their own evidence, not merely because H3 is supported.
